## Learning Objectives

By the end of this lesson you will be able to:

- **Represent** tabular data as vectors and matrices, and **read** an array's shape (rows by columns). *(Understand)*
- **Compute** a dot product — by hand and with `@` — and **interpret** it as a weighted sum and as a similarity score (including cosine). *(Apply)*
- **Interpret** the dot product and cosine geometrically — as an angle between arrows, a shadow, and direction without length — and **explain** why cosines of all-positive ratings are never negative and what mean-centering changes. *(Understand / Analyze)*
- **Apply** a matrix-vector product to score every item for one user, and a matrix-matrix product to score all users against all items at once. *(Apply)*
- **Predict** the shape of a product from the inner-dimension rule, and **use** transpose, the identity matrix, and projection onto a direction. *(Apply / Analyze)*

> **Where this sits:** a cross-cutting **foundations** primer, taught at the seam of Unit V — after the qualitative half (**L16** space, **L17** time) and right before the quantitative half. It is the toolkit that **L19** (correlation), **L20** (PCA), and **Unit VI** (recommenders) all run on.

## Why This Matters

The back half of this course looks like four unrelated topics — correlation,
dimensionality reduction (PCA), recommender systems, social-network graphs —
but underneath they run on the *same five operations*, and you have been
using the first one since L02 without naming it. "How alike are two users?"
is a **dot product**. "Score every movie for one user" is a **matrix times a
vector**. "Predict every user's rating of every movie" is a **matrix times a
matrix**. None of this requires the linear-algebra course you may not have
taken — just the handful of operations below, all one line each in NumPy.

Each operation also has a **picture**. A user is an arrow; "how alike" is
the angle between two arrows; a dot product is the shadow one arrow casts on
another. Once you can see the picture, the formulas stop being arbitrary.

This is a foundations primer: small, operational, no proofs. We drill the
operations on a movie-ratings world tiny enough to check by hand, so that
when L20 *projects* data onto a new axis or a recommender *multiplies*
user-factors by item-factors, the machinery is already familiar.

## Data as Vectors and Matrices

> **Analogy:** a **vector** is one row of a spreadsheet — a list of numbers
> in order. A **matrix** is the whole sheet — a grid of numbers, rows by
> columns. NumPy stores both in the `ndarray` you met in L02.

Take four users rating five movies from 1 to 5. The whole table is a
**matrix** `R` with shape `(4, 5)` — 4 rows (users), 5 columns (movies). One
user's ratings are a **vector** — a single row.

```python
import numpy as np

#               Action1 Action2 Romance1 Romance2 Comedy
R = np.array([[5, 4, 1, 1, 3],    # Ana   -- action fan
              [4, 5, 2, 1, 2],    # Beto  -- action fan
              [1, 1, 5, 4, 3],    # Carla -- romance fan
              [2, 1, 4, 5, 3]])   # Dani  -- romance fan

R.shape        # (4, 5)  -> (rows, cols) = (users, movies)
R[0]           # array([5, 4, 1, 1, 3])  -- Ana's row, a vector
R[:, 2]        # array([1, 2, 5, 4])     -- the Romance1 column
R[0, 4]        # 3  -- Ana's rating of Comedy
```

The **shape** `(rows, cols)` is the single most important thing to track:
nearly every linear-algebra bug is a shape that did not line up. Say the
shape out loud before every operation.

## The Dot Product

The **dot product** of two equal-length vectors multiplies them
element-by-element and adds up the results — one number out:

```python
ana, beto, carla = R[0], R[1], R[2]
np.sum(ana * beto)   # 49   -- elementwise multiply, then sum
np.dot(ana, beto)    # 49   -- the same thing, named
ana @ beto           # 49   -- the @ operator, the usual way to write it
```

That single number has two readings, and both run the back half of the
course:

- **A weighted sum.** $a \cdot b = \sum_i a_i b_i$. If `b` is a vector of
  weights, `a @ b` is "combine the entries of `a` with those weights" — how
  a model turns features into one score.
- **A similarity score.** Two vectors that are large in the same positions
  produce a big dot product. `Ana @ Beto = 49` (both love action) beats
  `Ana @ Carla = 27` (tastes diverge).

Why should "multiply and add" measure similarity at all? The answer is
geometric, and it is worth a picture.

## The Geometry: Arrows, Angles, and Shadows

A vector with two numbers is a point on a plane — or, better, an **arrow**
from the origin to that point. Describe each user by two *taste* numbers:
how much they like action, and how much they like romance. Ana's taste is
`[1.0, 0.2]` (all action), Carla's is `[0.2, 1.0]` (all romance). Drawn as
arrows, they point in clearly different directions:

![Two panels in a plane with an action axis and a romance axis. Left: a red arrow for Ana's taste, 1.0 action and 0.2 romance, points almost along the action axis; a blue arrow for Carla's taste, 0.2 action and 1.0 romance, points almost straight up. An arc between them is labeled theta = 67.4 degrees; the title says both arrows have length 1.02 and the cosine of the angle is 0.385. Right: the same two arrows, with a dashed line dropped at a right angle from the tip of Carla's arrow onto Ana's direction. The segment from the origin to where it lands is drawn in green and labeled "shadow of b on a: 0.392"; the title reads a dot b = shadow times length of a = 0.392 times 1.020 = 0.40.](assets/l18_angle_shadow.png)

The dot product has an equivalent **geometric** formula. For two arrows of
lengths $\lVert a \rVert$ and $\lVert b \rVert$ with angle $\theta$ between
them:

$$a \cdot b = \lVert a \rVert \, \lVert b \rVert \cos\theta$$

where the **length** (or **norm**) of a vector is
$\lVert a \rVert = \sqrt{a \cdot a}$ — Pythagoras, in any number of
dimensions. Check it on the picture: the "multiply and add" recipe gives
$1.0 \times 0.2 + 0.2 \times 1.0 = 0.40$, and the geometric formula gives
$1.02 \times 1.02 \times \cos 67.4^\circ = 0.40$ — the same number, read two
ways.

**Reading the right panel:** drop a line from the tip of `b` straight down
onto `a`'s direction. The green segment is `b`'s **shadow** on `a` — how far
`b` reaches *in `a`'s direction*. The dot product is that shadow times the
length of `a`. So a big dot product means "the two arrows reach the same
way," which is exactly why it scores similarity.

The shadow also explains the **sign** of a dot product:

![Three panels, each with a black arrow a pointing right and a blue arrow b of the same length. Left, titled same direction: b is 40 degrees above a, its shadow falls on a's side in green, and a dot b = +0.77, positive. Middle, titled perpendicular: b points straight up at 90 degrees, it casts no shadow, and a dot b = 0. Right, titled opposite: b is at 140 degrees, its shadow falls behind the origin in purple, and a dot b = -0.77, negative.](assets/l18_dot_sign.png)

- **Same general direction** (angle under 90 degrees): the shadow points
  along `a`, and the dot product is **positive**.
- **Perpendicular** (exactly 90 degrees): no shadow at all, and the dot
  product is **zero**. Such vectors are called **orthogonal** — for tastes,
  "unrelated": neither leans toward the other, nor against it.
- **Opposite** (angle over 90 degrees): the shadow points backward, and the
  dot product is **negative**.

**Try it.** Turn and stretch `b` and watch the dot product follow its shadow.
Arrow `a` is fixed at Ana's taste `[1.0, 0.2]`.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof dotAngle = Inputs.range([0, 180], {value: 67, step: 1, label: "angle between a and b (degrees)"})
viewof dotLength = Inputs.range([0.25, 1.5], {value: 1, step: 0.05, label: "length of b"})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
dotExplorer = {
  const W = 340, s = 120, cx = 170, cy = 190;
  const X = (x) => cx + s * x, Y = (y) => cy - s * y;
  const a = [1.0, 0.2];
  const na = Math.hypot(a[0], a[1]);
  const ta = Math.atan2(a[1], a[0]);
  const t = ta + dotAngle * Math.PI / 180;
  const b = [dotLength * Math.cos(t), dotLength * Math.sin(t)];
  const dot = a[0] * b[0] + a[1] * b[1];
  const shadow = dot / na;
  const u = [a[0] / na, a[1] / na];
  const foot = [shadow * u[0], shadow * u[1]];
  const isZero = dotAngle === 90;
  const col = isZero ? "gray" : (dot > 0 ? "seagreen" : "darkorchid");
  // ticks every 0.5 (with faint grid lines) so coordinates can be read off the picture
  const xTicks = [-1, -0.5, 0.5, 1], yTicks = [-0.5, 0.5, 1, 1.5];
  const grid = [
    ...xTicks.map((v) => htl.svg`<line x1="${X(v)}" y1="0" x2="${X(v)}" y2="${W - 40}" stroke="#eee" stroke-width="1"></line>`),
    ...yTicks.map((v) => htl.svg`<line x1="0" y1="${Y(v)}" x2="${W}" y2="${Y(v)}" stroke="#eee" stroke-width="1"></line>`)
  ];
  // tick marks sit on the axes; their labels sit on the bottom and left edges,
  // where the arrows and the shadow cannot cover them
  const ticks = [
    ...xTicks.map((v) => htl.svg`<line x1="${X(v)}" y1="${cy - 4}" x2="${X(v)}" y2="${cy + 4}" stroke="#888" stroke-width="1"></line>
      <text x="${X(v)}" y="${W - 46}" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#666">${v}</text>`),
    ...yTicks.map((v) => htl.svg`<line x1="${cx - 4}" y1="${Y(v)}" x2="${cx + 4}" y2="${Y(v)}" stroke="#888" stroke-width="1"></line>
      <text x="3" y="${Y(v) + 4}" text-anchor="start" font-size="11" fill="#666">${v}</text>`)
  ];
  const r = 0.28;
  const arc = `M ${X(r * Math.cos(ta))} ${Y(r * Math.sin(ta))} A ${s * r} ${s * r} 0 0 0 ${X(r * Math.cos(t))} ${Y(r * Math.sin(t))}`;
  const pic = htl.svg`<svg width="${W}" height="${W - 40}" viewBox="0 0 ${W} ${W - 40}" style="max-width: 100%; height: auto; font-family: sans-serif;">
    <defs>
      <marker id="l18-head-a" viewBox="0 0 10 10" refX="9" refY="5" markerWidth="7" markerHeight="7" orient="auto-start-reverse"><path d="M 0 0 L 10 5 L 0 10 z" fill="crimson"></path></marker>
      <marker id="l18-head-b" viewBox="0 0 10 10" refX="9" refY="5" markerWidth="7" markerHeight="7" orient="auto-start-reverse"><path d="M 0 0 L 10 5 L 0 10 z" fill="steelblue"></path></marker>
    </defs>
    ${grid}
    <line x1="0" y1="${cy}" x2="${W}" y2="${cy}" stroke="#bbb" stroke-width="1"></line>
    <line x1="${cx}" y1="0" x2="${cx}" y2="${W - 40}" stroke="#bbb" stroke-width="1"></line>
    ${ticks}
    <line x1="${X(-1.4 * u[0])}" y1="${Y(-1.4 * u[1])}" x2="${X(1.4 * u[0])}" y2="${Y(1.4 * u[1])}" stroke="crimson" stroke-width="1" stroke-dasharray="2 4"></line>
    <line x1="${X(0)}" y1="${Y(0)}" x2="${X(foot[0])}" y2="${Y(foot[1])}" stroke="${col}" stroke-width="9" stroke-opacity="0.75"></line>
    <line x1="${X(b[0])}" y1="${Y(b[1])}" x2="${X(foot[0])}" y2="${Y(foot[1])}" stroke="gray" stroke-width="1.2" stroke-dasharray="5 4"></line>
    <path d="${arc}" fill="none" stroke="black" stroke-width="1.2"></path>
    <line x1="${X(0)}" y1="${Y(0)}" x2="${X(a[0])}" y2="${Y(a[1])}" stroke="crimson" stroke-width="3" marker-end="url(#l18-head-a)"></line>
    <line x1="${X(0)}" y1="${Y(0)}" x2="${X(b[0])}" y2="${Y(b[1])}" stroke="steelblue" stroke-width="3" marker-end="url(#l18-head-b)"></line>
    <text x="${X(a[0]) + 6}" y="${Y(a[1]) + 18}" fill="crimson" font-weight="bold" font-size="15">a</text>
    <text x="${X(b[0]) + 6}" y="${Y(b[1]) - 6}" fill="steelblue" font-weight="bold" font-size="15">b</text>
  </svg>`;
  const kind = isZero ? "zero: orthogonal" : (dot > 0 ? "positive" : "negative");
  const fmt = (x) => (isZero && Math.abs(x) < 1e-9 ? 0 : x).toFixed(3);
  const lab = "padding-right: 1.5em;";
  const table = htl.html`<table style="font-family: monospace; font-size: 0.95rem; margin-top: 0.5rem;">
    <tr><td style="${lab}">|a|</td><td style="text-align: right;">${na.toFixed(3)}</td></tr>
    <tr><td style="${lab}">|b|</td><td style="text-align: right;">${dotLength.toFixed(3)}</td></tr>
    <tr><td style="${lab}">cos(angle)</td><td style="text-align: right;">${fmt(Math.cos(dotAngle * Math.PI / 180))}</td></tr>
    <tr><td style="${lab}">shadow of b on a</td><td style="text-align: right;">${fmt(shadow)}</td></tr>
    <tr><td style="${lab}"><b>a &middot; b</b></td><td style="text-align: right;"><b>${fmt(dot)}</b></td></tr>
    <tr><td colspan="2" style="color: ${col};">${kind}</td></tr>
  </table>`;
  return htl.html`<div style="display: flex; flex-wrap: wrap; gap: 1.5rem; align-items: center;">${pic}${table}</div>`;
}
```

**Reading the widget:** at 90 degrees the shadow vanishes and `a · b` hits
zero; past 90 it turns purple and negative. Stretching `b` changes the dot
product but **not** the angle or its cosine — which is the cue for the next
section.

## Cosine Similarity: Direction, Not Length

Raw dot products are inflated by length — someone who rates everything 5
looks "similar" to everyone. To measure only *direction*, solve the
geometric formula for the angle. That is **cosine similarity**:

$$\cos(a, b) = \frac{a \cdot b}{\lVert a \rVert \, \lVert b \rVert}$$

```python
def cosine(a, b):
    return a @ b / (np.linalg.norm(a) * np.linalg.norm(b))

cosine(ana, beto)    # 0.961  -- two action fans: nearly the same direction
cosine(ana, carla)   # 0.519  -- action vs romance: pulling apart

np.degrees(np.arccos(cosine(ana, beto)))    # 16.1  -- degrees apart
np.degrees(np.arccos(cosine(ana, carla)))   # 58.7
```

![Two panels in the action-romance plane. Left: Ana's red taste arrow, a longer faint red arrow labeled 2 x Ana pointing the same way, and Carla's blue arrow. The title reports Ana dot Carla = 0.40 but 2 x Ana dot Carla = 0.80, while the cosine is 0.385 for both, the same angle. Right: a unit circle with all four users' arrows shrunk to length 1: Ana and Beto almost on top of each other near the action axis, Carla and Dani almost on top of each other near the romance axis. The title says dividing each vector by its length puts every user on the unit circle, and the cosine is the dot product of those arrows.](assets/l18_direction_length.png)

**Reading the figure:** doubling Ana's arrow doubles the dot product
(0.40 to 0.80) but leaves the angle, and so the cosine (0.385), unchanged.
Dividing by the two lengths is the same as first shrinking every arrow to
length 1 — onto the **unit circle** on the right — and then taking an
ordinary dot product. Cosine keeps the *direction* of taste and throws away
its *intensity*.

The ratings rows have **five** numbers, so you cannot draw them on paper —
but the angle is still real. Any two arrows, in any number of dimensions,
lie together in one flat plane through the origin, and within that plane
they make an ordinary angle. That is why `cosine(ana, beto)` can say
"16.1 degrees apart" about five-number vectors. A clean **0.96 vs 0.52**:
the normalized dot product answers "how alike are two users?" — the engine
of the recommenders in Unit VI.

## The Positive Corner, and Shifting the Origin

Look again at that 0.52. Ana and Carla have *opposite* tastes, yet their
cosine is comfortably positive. The picture says why:

![Five arrows in a plane whose axes are the Action1 rating and the Romance1 rating. The positive quarter of the plane is shaded. Ana (5, 1) and Beto (4, 2) point to the lower right in red, Carla (1, 5) and Dani (2, 4) to the upper left in blue, and Eva (5, 5) in orange runs along a dashed diagonal line labeled "rates both the same". The angle between Ana and Carla is marked 67.4 degrees. A note below the corner says every arrow lives in this corner, so no two are more than 90 degrees apart.](assets/l18_positive_corner.png)

(The figure keeps just two movies, Action1 and Romance1, so you can see it;
on those two Ana and Carla are 67.4 degrees apart, on all five 58.7.)
Ratings are positive numbers, so every user's arrow lives in the **positive
corner** of the space. Two arrows in that corner can never be more than 90
degrees apart, so their cosine can never go negative — even for opposite
tastes. It gets worse at the **diagonal**. Meet **Eva**, who rates every
movie 5: her arrow runs right down the middle of the corner, close to
everyone.

```python
eva = np.array([5, 5, 5, 5, 5])
R @ eva                           # array([70, 70, 70, 75])
[cosine(r, eva) for r in R]       # 0.868, 0.885, 0.868, 0.905
```

Eva's raw dot product with every user (70 to 75) beats Ana and Beto's 49 —
by that measure she is everyone's soulmate. Cosine tames her, but only
partly: she still scores 0.87 to 0.91 with everyone, because she sits on the
diagonal and the diagonal is near every arrow in the corner. What we
actually care about is not "rates movies highly" but "rates movies
*differently from their own average*" — what each user is *for* and
*against*.

The fix is to **shift the origin**. Subtract each user's own average rating
from their row — **mean-centering**. Now an above-average rating is
positive, a below-average one is negative, and the arrows can leave the
corner:

```python
# Subtract each user's own average. keepdims=True keeps the 4 averages
# as a column, so row i loses its own average.
R_c = R - R.mean(axis=1, keepdims=True)

R_c[0]                   # array([ 2.2,  1.2, -1.8, -1.8,  0.2])  -- Ana
cosine(R_c[0], R_c[2])   # -0.953  -- Ana vs Carla: now nearly opposite
cosine(R_c[0], R_c[1])   #  0.834  -- Ana vs Beto: still alike
```

**Reading the output:** Ana and Carla jump from **+0.519 to -0.953** — the
numbers finally say what the tastes say, opposite. Ana and Beto drop a little
(0.961 to 0.834) because their shared habit of rating above the middle no
longer counts as agreement. And Eva? Every one of her ratings equals her
average, so centering turns her into the **zero vector**, an arrow of length
zero, and her cosine is undefined (0 divided by 0). That is the honest
answer: a user who rates everything the same tells you nothing about taste.

Geometrically, centering does one thing: it **projects every arrow onto the
directions perpendicular to the diagonal**, where "rates everything higher"
no longer exists. With three movies those directions form a flat plane, so
you can rotate it yourself, with the three movies as the three axes:

::: {.panel-tabset}

## Rotate it (interactive)

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
Plotly = require("https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/plotly.js-dist-min@2.35.2/plotly.min.js")
viewof cornerMode = Inputs.radio(["raw ratings", "mean-centered"], {value: "raw ratings", label: "Show"})
viewof cornerPlane = Inputs.toggle({label: "shade the plane through Ana and Carla", value: false})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
cornerPlot = {
  const names = ["Ana", "Beto", "Carla", "Dani", "Eva"];
  const colors = ["crimson", "crimson", "steelblue", "steelblue", "darkorange"];
  // Action1, Action2, Romance1 ratings (columns 0, 1, 2 of R) plus Eva
  const raw = [[5, 4, 1], [4, 5, 2], [1, 1, 5], [2, 1, 4], [5, 5, 5]];
  const centered = cornerMode === "mean-centered";
  const vecs = raw.map((v) => {
    const m = (v[0] + v[1] + v[2]) / 3;
    return centered ? v.map((x) => x - m) : v;
  });
  const dot = (p, q) => p[0] * q[0] + p[1] * q[1] + p[2] * q[2];
  const cosAC = dot(vecs[0], vecs[2]) / Math.sqrt(dot(vecs[0], vecs[0]) * dot(vecs[2], vecs[2]));
  const traces = vecs.map((v, i) => ({
    type: "scatter3d", mode: "lines+markers+text", name: names[i],
    x: [0, v[0]], y: [0, v[1]], z: [0, v[2]],
    text: ["", (centered && i === 4) ? "Eva = 0" : names[i]], textposition: "top center",
    textfont: {color: colors[i], size: 14},
    line: {color: colors[i], width: 7}, marker: {color: colors[i], size: [0, 5]},
    hoverinfo: "text", hovertext: ["origin", names[i] + " (" + v.map((x) => x.toFixed(2)).join(", ") + ")"]
  }));
  const lim = centered ? 3 : 5.5;
  const lo = centered ? -3 : 0;
  // the diagonal: "rates all three movies the same"
  traces.push({type: "scatter3d", mode: "lines", x: [lo, lim], y: [lo, lim], z: [lo, lim],
               line: {color: "gray", width: 3, dash: "dash"}, hoverinfo: "text", hovertext: "the diagonal"});
  if (centered) {
    // the plane x + y + z = 0, perpendicular to the diagonal
    const e1 = [1 / Math.SQRT2, -1 / Math.SQRT2, 0];
    const e2 = [1 / Math.sqrt(6), 1 / Math.sqrt(6), -2 / Math.sqrt(6)];
    const c = [[3, 3], [-3, 3], [-3, -3], [3, -3]].map(([p, q]) => e1.map((x, k) => p * x + q * e2[k]));
    traces.push({type: "mesh3d", x: c.map((p) => p[0]), y: c.map((p) => p[1]), z: c.map((p) => p[2]),
                 i: [0, 0], j: [1, 2], k: [2, 3], color: "gray", opacity: 0.15, hoverinfo: "skip"});
  }
  if (cornerPlane) {
    const a = vecs[0], b = vecs[2];
    const p = [[0, 0, 0], a, a.map((x, k) => x + b[k]), b];
    traces.push({type: "mesh3d", x: p.map((q) => q[0]), y: p.map((q) => q[1]), z: p.map((q) => q[2]),
                 i: [0, 0], j: [1, 2], k: [2, 3], color: "goldenrod", opacity: 0.35, hoverinfo: "skip"});
  }
  const axis = (title) => ({title: {text: title}, range: [lo, lim]});
  const layout = {
    height: 480, margin: {l: 0, r: 0, t: 10, b: 0}, showlegend: false,
    scene: {xaxis: axis("Action1"), yaxis: axis("Action2"), zaxis: axis("Romance1"), aspectmode: "cube",
            // centered: look almost straight down the diagonal, so the plane faces the reader
            camera: {eye: centered ? {x: 1.5, y: 1.1, z: 1.3} : {x: 1.6, y: -1.6, z: 0.9}}}
  };
  const div = htl.html`<div style="width: 100%; max-width: 640px;"></div>`;
  const note = htl.html`<p style="font-family: monospace;">cos(Ana, Carla) in these three movies = ${cosAC.toFixed(3)}
    (${(Math.acos(cosAC) * 180 / Math.PI).toFixed(1)} degrees apart)</p>`;
  const wrap = htl.html`<div>${div}${note}</div>`;
  yield wrap;
  await Plotly.newPlot(div, traces, layout, {displaylogo: false, responsive: true});
}
```

Drag to rotate; scroll to zoom. Switch between raw and centered, and turn on
the plane through Ana and Carla.

## Static view

![Two 3-D plots with axes Action1, Action2 and Romance1. Left, raw ratings: five arrows from the origin all crowd into the positive corner around a dashed diagonal; Eva in orange lies right on the diagonal; the title gives cos(Ana, Carla) = +0.416. Right, mean-centered: the arrows now lie on one flat gray plane through the origin, the red action fans Ana and Beto point one way, the blue romance fans Carla and Dani point the opposite way, and Eva has collapsed to a dot at the origin labeled Eva = 0; the title gives cos(Ana, Carla) = -0.971.](assets/l18_centering_3d.png)

:::

**Reading the 3-D view:** raw, all five arrows huddle around the diagonal,
and the Ana-Carla cosine is +0.416 in these three movies. Centered, the
arrows drop onto the plane perpendicular to the diagonal, Eva collapses to
the origin, and the Ana-Carla cosine swings to -0.971: the action fans and the romance fans now
point in opposite directions. With the shaded plane on, you can see the
point made earlier — two arrows always share one flat plane, whatever the
number of dimensions.

This centered cosine has a famous name: it is the **correlation** between
the two users' ratings. **L19** builds it properly — centering *columns*
(variables) instead of rows (users), same geometry — and the
collaborative-filtering recommenders of **L22** compare users exactly this
way.

## Matrix times Vector

A dot product compares *two* vectors. A **matrix-vector product** does one
dot product for *every row of the matrix at once*. Give each movie two
feature scores — how much *action* and how much *romance* it has — in a
matrix `F` with shape `(5, 2)`, and give one user a taste vector `w` (how
much they like action vs romance). Then `F @ w` scores all five movies in a
single multiply:

```python
F = np.array([[1.0, 0.0],    # Action1   [action, romance]
              [0.9, 0.1],    # Action2
              [0.0, 1.0],    # Romance1
              [0.1, 0.9],    # Romance2
              [0.5, 0.5]])   # Comedy
w_ana = np.array([1.0, 0.2])     # Ana loves action, mild on romance

F @ w_ana    # array([1.  , 0.92, 0.2 , 0.28, 0.6 ])
```

Each entry is one dot product — row of `F` with `w` — so Action1 scores
`1.0` and Romance1 only `0.2`. One operation, every item scored for this
user. The shapes tell you it will work: `(5, 2) @ (2,) -> (5,)`. The rule:

::: {.callout-important title="The inner-dimension rule"}
A product `A @ B` is legal only when the **inner** dimensions match:
`(m, n) @ (n, p) -> (m, p)`. The shared `n` cancels; the result keeps the
**outer** dimensions `m` and `p`. Here `(5, 2) @ (2,)` shares the `2`, so
the result has length `5`. Mismatched inner dimensions are the single most
common linear-algebra error — and NumPy raises a `ValueError` rather than
guessing.
:::

**The same picture again.** Draw each movie as a point in the
action-romance plane and the user's taste `w` as a direction. Each score is
the movie's shadow on that direction (times the length of `w`), so ranking
the movies for a user means **lining up their shadows on the user's taste
direction**. Turn the taste direction and the ranking turns with it — the
lab lets you do exactly that with a slider.

## Matrix times Matrix

Stack many users' taste vectors into a matrix and you can score *all users
against all items in one shot*. This is **matrix-matrix multiplication**,
and it is exactly how recommender systems work (Unit VI): a **user-factor**
matrix `U` (each user's taste, `4 x 2`) times an **item-factor** matrix `V`
(each movie's features, `2 x 5`) gives a full table of predicted ratings.

We already have the item features in `F` (shape `5 x 2`); we need them as
`2 x 5`, which is the **transpose** `F.T` — rows become columns:

```python
U = np.array([[1.0, 0.2],    # Ana    [action-taste, romance-taste]
              [0.9, 0.1],    # Beto
              [0.2, 1.0],    # Carla
              [0.1, 0.9]])   # Dani
V = F.T          # shape (2, 5): the two factors as rows

R_hat = U @ V    # (4, 2) @ (2, 5) -> (4, 5): every user x every movie
```

`R_hat[0]` comes out `[1.0, 0.92, 0.2, 0.28, 0.6]` — *identical* to the
matrix-vector score we computed for Ana alone. Matrix-matrix multiplication
is just the matrix-vector product run for every user at once. That single
`U @ V` — predicting all ratings from compact factors — is the heart of
**matrix factorization**, the recommender technique of Unit VI.

## Transpose, Identity, and Shapes

Three small tools round out the kit:

- **Transpose** (`A.T`) flips rows and columns: `(5, 2)` becomes `(2, 5)`.
  Use it to make inner dimensions line up (as we did to build `V` from `F`).
- **Identity matrix** (`np.eye(n)`) is the "do-nothing" matrix — 1s on the
  diagonal, 0s elsewhere. `A @ I == A`, the matrix version of multiplying
  by 1. It is the reference point for "undoing" a matrix (the matrix
  inverse, which this course does not cover).
- **Shapes** are the contract. Read them before every `@`: if the inner
  dimensions match, the product exists and you already know its shape.

```python
F.T.shape            # (2, 5)
F @ np.eye(2)        # == F  (the identity changes nothing)
# (4, 2) @ (2, 5) -> (4, 5)   inner 2 == 2, OK
# (4, 2) @ (4, 2) -> ValueError: inner 2 != 4
```

## Projection: a Peek at PCA

You have already seen projection: it is the **shadow** from the geometry
section. Take a **unit** direction vector `d` (length 1). Then `point @ d`
is the length of the point's shadow on that direction — *where the point
falls along that axis*, a single number that summarizes a multi-dimensional
point by one coordinate. With length 1 there is nothing to rescale: the dot
product *is* the shadow.

Project each user's 2-D taste vector onto the "action-versus-romance" axis
`d = [1, -1]/sqrt(2)`:

```python
d = np.array([1.0, -1.0]) / np.sqrt(2)
U @ d    # array([ 0.566,  0.566, -0.566, -0.566])
#          Ana    Beto    Carla   Dani
```

![Scatter plot of four users in a two-dimensional space whose axes are an action factor and a romance factor. Ana and Beto sit in red at the lower-right (high action, low romance); Carla and Dani sit in blue at the upper-left (low action, high romance). A dashed gray diagonal line runs from upper-left to lower-right through the origin, the projection axis; thin lines drop each user onto that axis, where the two red points land together on the positive side and the two blue points land together on the negative side.](assets/l18_projection.png)

**Reading the output:** two numbers — `+0.566` for the action fans, `-0.566`
for the romance fans — separate the four users on a *single* axis. We turned
a 2-D dataset into 1-D and kept the structure that mattered. That is exactly
what **PCA** (L20) does, except PCA *finds* the most informative direction
for you instead of being handed one. Projection is a dot product; PCA is
projection onto a cleverly chosen `d`.

## When to Use Which / Common Pitfalls

- **`@` is not `*`.** `a * b` multiplies element by element (same shape out);
  `a @ b` is the dot/matrix product (dimensions collapse). Reaching for `*`
  when you meant `@` is the classic first-week bug.
- **Shape mismatch.** `A @ B` needs `A.shape[1] == B.shape[0]`. When NumPy
  raises a `ValueError`, print both shapes and check the inner pair — often
  a missing `.T`.
- **Row vs column orientation.** A 1-D array `(n,)` works on either side of
  `@` — NumPy infers whether it should act as a row or a column. (Explicit
  2-D column vectors `(n, 1)` are stricter about shape, but you will not need
  them here.)
- **Unnormalized similarity.** A raw dot product rewards long arrows; for
  "how alike" use cosine, which keeps only the direction.
- **All-positive data never looks opposite.** Ratings, counts, and prices
  live in the positive corner, so their cosines stay at or above 0 even for
  opposite tastes. If "opposite" should show up as negative, mean-center
  first.
- **The zero vector has no direction.** A row that is all zeros (or all one
  value, after centering) gives 0 divided by 0, and NumPy returns `nan` with
  a warning. Check for it before ranking by cosine.

## FAQ / Industry Reality

**"Do I need eigenvalues, determinants, and matrix inverses?"** — Not for
this course. Those are the deeper layer (and the reason a full linear-algebra
course exists); PCA's *derivation* uses eigenvectors, but you will *run* PCA
with one scikit-learn call in L20. This primer is deliberately the operational
subset: the operations you will actually type.

**"Is an angle between 5-number vectors real, or just a metaphor?"** — Real.
Any two vectors span one flat plane through the origin, and inside that
plane they make an ordinary angle; cosine measures it. The same is true for
the 1,682-movie rating vectors of L22. You only
lose the ability to *draw* all the vectors at once.

**"Is `@` just `*` for arrays?"** — No, and confusing them is the most common
NumPy mistake. `*` is elementwise (shapes unchanged); `@` is the dot/matrix
product (dimensions contract by the inner-dimension rule). Different math,
different output shape.

**"Why NumPy instead of Python loops?"** — The same reason as L02: a matrix
multiply is one vectorized C-level call over the whole array, hundreds of
times faster than nested Python loops, and it reads as the math it is.

## Cheat-sheet

| Task | NumPy |
|---|---|
| Make a matrix / read its shape | `np.array([[...], [...]])` · `A.shape` |
| Grab a row (vector) / a column | `A[i]` · `A[:, j]` |
| Dot product of two vectors | `a @ b` (or `np.dot(a, b)`) |
| Vector length (norm) | `np.linalg.norm(a)` |
| Unit vector (same direction, length 1) | `a / np.linalg.norm(a)` |
| Cosine similarity | `a @ b / (norm(a) * norm(b))` |
| Angle in degrees | `np.degrees(np.arccos(cos))` |
| Mean-center each row | `R - R.mean(axis=1, keepdims=True)` |
| Score all items for one user | `F @ w` (matrix x vector) |
| Score all users x all items | `U @ V` (matrix x matrix) |
| Transpose / identity | `A.T` · `np.eye(n)` |
| Project onto a unit direction | `points @ d` |
